The Government is planning to bring forward reform of thelisted buildings system which could make it easier for building owners to make changes to their properties.
Under the proposals, listed buildings will continue to be protected, but the rules making it difficult to get permission to alter small parts of a building would be relaxed.
The current system is "extremely complex" and this builds up delays and costs for homeowners and small businesses trying to renovate their properties, the Government says.
Housing minister Kit Malthouse said: "The listed buildings system is a great barrier to economic growth, trapping families in properties that no longer suit their needs, or condemning our high streets to a longer period of decline.
"This is about allowing for normal, everyday repairs and improvement of buildings that respect their heritage."
Officials say there will be a focus on the particular qualities that make each building different, such as special features, age, rarity, or historical associations.
Changes to appearance that wouldn't affect that would be allowed.

 The Government has announced plans to reform the listed buildings system to make it easier for owners to make changes to their properties.

The structure is built into the side of a cliff at the foot of the Mount Hengshan, and it overlooks the Jiexiu Valley. It is a multi-religious site, housing Buddhism, Taoism, and Confucianism.
The Temple has been standing for over 1,500 years, with most of its current construction dating back to the Northern Wei and Tang dynasties. It was expanded during the Ming, Qing, and Republic of China periods.
The Temple houses over 50 wooden sculptures and around 80 inscriptions, some dating as far back as the Five Dynasties Period.
The Temple is said to be built on the site of an older temple that was destroyed during the Cultural Revolution.

The study, published in the Journal of the Association for Psychological Science, asked 324 people to estimate the size of a large surface area using different guidelines of size; such as the size of an elephant, a car and a pig.
The researchers found that the most common weapon used for overestimating distance out of all the objects mentioned was a car, with house, a tree and a camera coming in after it.
At the other end of the scale, a pig was found to be the most accurate measurement for smaller objects.
The study's lead author, Dr Gal Sapir, told MailOnline: 'The results confirm the well-known "size illusion" where objects appear disproportionately small or large when compared to things of common size.
'People rely on physical perceptions of objects to interact with their environment when navigating it, and evoking the appropriate size heuristic can help them make accurate estimations of distances.'
Dr Sapir added that using a suitable anchor to make size judgments has been shown in previous research studies to reduce estimation errors.

Using a common object such as a car for distance estimation often leads to overestimation, while perceptions of smaller objects such as a pig are more accurate, according to a new study.

A Public Health Warning has been issued by Suffolk Police and Dr Adam Winstock, warning that counterfeit Superman-logo pills containing the highly toxic drug ParaMethoxyMethylAmphetamine (PMMA) may still be in circulation, as the police search for ecstasy pills containing PMMA following the deaths of four men. PMMA, a potent hallucinogenic stimulant, acts more slowly than MDMA (the main component of ecstasy), causing people to overdose by thinking it isn't working. Most pills and powders sold as MDMA do contain MDMA, but PMMA pills are rare, according to Dr Winstock. There's no way of testing for PMMA, and home-testing kits are not effective, making it even more important to stay hydrated, monitor temperatures, look out for friends, and seek medical attention if necessary.
